transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Alex Perkins (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Marcos Rivera (Helios - Lead ML Eng), Priya Desai (Helios - Infra), Ethan Cole (Product), Jia Li (Security)

Summary (auto): deep technical review of Redwood KV cache behavior under long-context payments ingestion workload; focus on eviction, paging, prefix reuse, and tuning recommendations for VPC/on-prem deployment.

[00:00] Alex Perkins: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Alex from Redwood here, I'll hand it off to Samira in a bit but quick agenda: run through the Helios workload you sent, show relevant KV cache internals, discuss observed evictions and paging, and map to config changes and follow-ups.
[00:28] Marcos Rivera: Thanks Alex. Quick context: our models serve multi-turn fraud detection prompts, often 8k to 50k tokens of conversation and historical transaction context. We're seeing odd latency spikes and cache thrash — sessions that should reuse prefixes are not, and our cost is spiking.
[00:47] Samira Khan: Got it. When you say 50k, is that long context concatenated or streaming?
[00:55] Marcos Rivera: It's a mix — prefix history stored and then we append the 2-4k token latest window. Some calls are increasing to >60k in a single trace.
[01:12] Priya Desai: For infra, we're on a dedicated Redwood Dedicated pool in our VPC, GPUs are A100-ish, and we run quantized model builds (8-bit) for cost. We also use prefix reuse aggressively to save compute.
[01:28] Alex Perkins: Good — that helps. Samira, want to sketch the KV cache layout for folks?
[01:33] Samira Khan: Sure. High level: Redwood's runtime keeps a per-device KV cache for past key/values keyed by session-id+prefix-hash. We maintain a hot-set in GPU DRAM and a cold-set we page out to host memory or spill to disk depending on config. Eviction is LRU-ish with heuristics for prefix reuse; we also support pinning for critical prefixes.
[01:58] Samira Khan: Two common surprises: 1) very long contexts cause the cache to exceed DRAM fast, triggering paging which can add latency jitter, and 2) slight hash collision or session-id mismatch can prevent prefix reuse so you miss cache hits.
[02:18] Marcos Rivera: We're seeing a lot of paging; sometimes the tail latencies jump x10 for random requests. Is that the host spill?
[02:26] Samira Khan: Probably. Paging to host memory is much cheaper than disk but still 10-100ms overhead per page depending on size and concurrency. If it spills to NVMe it's worse.
[02:34] Ethan Cole: We saw distinct periods where throughput dropped and the console showed high evictions per-minute. Any idea why evictions spike?
[02:42] Samira Khan: Evictions spike when the working set exceeds the hot DRAM pool or when many unique prefixes are touched in a short window — e.g., many different user sessions with long contexts. Also aggressive batching can surface more unique KV slices at once.
[02:58] Priya Desai: We use adaptive batching tuned for throughput; maybe that interacts badly. Would reducing batch size help?
[03:05] Samira Khan: Possibly. Smaller batches reduce instantaneous memory pressure but cost more scheduling overhead. You can also prefer latency SLO by limiting max batch size or enabling prefix pinning for sessions you expect reuse on.
[03:18] Jia Li: From security: if we pin prefixes, are they encrypted in host memory and NVMe? We need KMS/HSM integration for private deployments.
[03:27] Alex Perkins: Yes — in Redwood Private/VPC we support KMS-based envelope encryption for spilled KV shards and audit logs for eviction/paging events. We'll share docs.
[03:36] Marcos Rivera: Can you explain prefix reuse mismatch? We believe our prefix hashing is consistent, but some calls still miss.
[03:44] Samira Khan: Common causes: session-id changes (cookie rotation or user-id hashing), whitespace/tokenization differences in your prefix generation, or subtle model tokenization drift if you've retrained/updated tokenizers. Also there is TTL heuristics — we sometimes age out prefixes if not accessed within N minutes.
[04:05] Marcos Rivera: Hmm TTL — what controls that?
[04:08] Samira Khan: There's a configurable ttl_window and hot_pool_size. Default is tuned for general web chat; for long-context workloads we recommend increasing hot_pool_size and lengthening ttl, but that increases GPU memory use.
[04:19] Marcos Rivera: Could we pin transaction-history prefixes for a given account and evict everything else more aggressively?
[04:24] Samira Khan: Yes, pinning is supported per-session or per-prefix pattern; pinned prefixes avoid eviction unless manually unpinned. That tradeoff is memory vs hit-rate.
[04:33] Priya Desai: Our concern is memory fragmentation and cross-tenant isolation in VPC. If we pin too many prefixes on host, will it affect other customers on same node?
[04:41] Alex Perkins: In Dedicated or Private you'll have tenant isolation options — we can allocate dedicated GPU pools per-customer. In shared-hosted, pins could affect co-tenants; we don't recommend pinning broadly on shared clusters.
[04:53] Samira Khan: Also important: prefix key composition matters. Use stable canonicalization — trim whitespace, normalize dates, consistent user-id salt. We can share a code snippet.
[05:04] Marcos Rivera: About eviction strategy — LRU feels simplistic for our workload since old but frequently reused prefixes (monthly statements) get evicted. Do you support ARC or frequency-aware policies?
[05:16] Samira Khan: We have an LFU-ish heuristic layered on top of LRU; there's also a frequency multiplier for prefixes with high reuse. Some customers have implemented a custom policy by tagging prefixes as 'hot' via API. ARC isn't native right now but we can simulate similar behavior with pinning + freq multipliers.
[05:33] Ethan Cole: What about paging granularity? Are we paging whole layers or chunked KV slices?
[05:39] Samira Khan: We page KV at slice granularity (per-layer per-head-block slices). That lets us fetch only what's needed for a prefix but can increase number of IO ops. We batch page-ins to mitigate latency.
[05:53] Priya Desai: You're saying batches of page-ins — do those block generation?
[05:58] Samira Khan: There is a wake-lock path: if a requested KV slice isn't in hot DRAM we schedule an async page-in and stall the generator until the slice materializes. The aim is to hide this with prefetching when we can predict reuse. Prefetch works well when prefix patterns are consistent.
[06:15] Marcos Rivera: Prefetch — can Redwood predict reuse for our fraud detection prefixes, which have periodic structures?
[06:21] Samira Khan: Yes, we can enable pattern-based prefetching. For instance, if you always prepend a transaction history block, we can prefetch those KV slices on session start. That reduces first-request latency but raises memory.
[06:33] Jia Li: Any privacy concerns with prefetching? Are those logs retained?
[06:36] Alex Perkins: Prefetching doesn't change retention rules; Redis/host cache segments can be configured to auto-expire and we support turning off telemetry for sensitive workloads. All persisted cache spill is encrypted under customer KMS in Private mode.
[06:52] Marcos Rivera: We saw a case where prefix reuse seemed to fail after a model update. Could tokenization differences be the reason?
[06:58] Samira Khan: Yes — model variant changes (different tokenizer or BPE merge tables) will alter tokenization and thus prefix hashes. We recommend pinning model+tokenizer versions in rollout and performing a small canonicalization test when swapping models.
[07:14] Marcos Rivera: That makes sense. In practice our ops people rotate model variants during canary and then promote; maybe we missed a tokenizer alignment.
[07:21] Samira Khan: Another tip: we support a 'compatibility shim' where you can compute a canonical prefix-hash on the client and pass it to Redwood to force reuse even across tokenizer minor differences, but that requires careful validation.
[07:36] Ethan Cole: Interesting. On the metrics side, what dashboards should we watch to correlate evictions with latency spikes?
[07:42] Samira Khan: Console metrics: cache_hit_rate, eviction_rate, page_in_latency_p50/p95, hot_pool_utilization, per-prefix_hit_counts. Correlate those with request latency p95 and batch_size trends.
[07:55] Priya Desai: We saw high page_in_latency_p95 during the 02:00 UTC batch job window — maybe scheduled jobs are causing working set churn.
[08:03] Marcos Rivera: We do nightly ingestion of transaction batches that touch a lot of unique prefixes. Could that be thrashing the cache?
[08:09] Samira Khan: Likely. For heavy ingestion windows we recommend either isolating batch jobs to a separate pool or throttling concurrency so you don't displace hot prefixes. Another option is to pre-warm expected prefixes into hot DRAM before peak online traffic.
[08:25] Marcos Rivera: Pre-warm — how long to pre-warm and what's the API?
[08:29] Samira Khan: You can call the cache_prefill API with a list of prefix hashes; pre-warm time depends on size but typically a few seconds per GB. We'll share sample scripts.
[08:40] Jia Li: For Private on-prem, is pre-warm IO bounded to local NVMe so it's faster?
[08:44] Samira Khan: Yes, local NVMe is faster than network attached storage. In on-prem we usually see page-in latencies much lower, but you must size NVMe and host DRAM appropriately.
[08:55] Alex Perkins: Quick question from my side: what's your acceptable p95 latency SLO and cost envelope?
[09:01] Marcos Rivera: Our p95 target for online fraud calls is <350ms for end-to-end inference; we can tolerate occasional 700ms but not sustained. Cost: we'd like to keep token-cost within current budget; moving to much larger hot pools would increase monthly spend significantly.
[09:16] Samira Khan: Understood. For p95 <350ms with long contexts, strategy: 1) enable prefix pinning for highest-value accounts, 2) prefetch predictable prefixes, 3) throttle batch ingestion to avoid hot set displacement, 4) tune quantization profile to reduce memory without hurting perf.
[09:33] Marcos Rivera: About quantization — we're running 8-bit and saw small accuracy regressions. Does quantization affect cache layout or page sizes?
[09:40] Samira Khan: Quantization affects per-KV slice size on memory; 8-bit reduces footprint which helps fit more in hot DRAM and reduces eviction. However, mixed precision or per-layer quant changes can shift memory distribution across layers which might change which slices get evicted first. Not a correctness issue for prefix reuse, just different memory pressure profile.
[09:59] Priya Desai: If we move to 4-bit quant or more aggressive compression, is compatibility with Redwood runtime good?
[10:05] Samira Khan: We have experimental 4-bit pipelines; they work with our runtime but you should run accuracy/latency bench. We'll flag them as beta for now. 4-bit helps fit larger hot pools but can increase compute latency on some kernels.
[10:18] Marcos Rivera: Any guidance on metrics to tradeoff memory vs latency?
[10:22] Samira Khan: Watch hot_pool_utilization and cache_hit_rate; if hit_rate increases when you increase hot_pool_size, you're in the right direction. Also measure page_in_p95 and end-to-end p95. We can run a 24-hour A/B with a small hot_pool bump to show impact.
[10:35] Ethan Cole: Can Redwood do a pilot with dedicated pool sizing recommendations?
[10:39] Alex Perkins: Yes — that's a common next step. We'll run a benchmark with your trace and recommend hot_pool_size, ttl, pin lists, and batching params.
[10:46] Marcos Rivera: About prefix hashing collisions — can we get a tool to simulate collision rates given our prefix distribution?
[10:51] Samira Khan: We'll share a small analyzer that computes prefix-hash entropy and flag likely collisions. Also check your session-id generation to avoid accidental reuse.
[10:59] Priya Desai: For VPC/on-prem, is there a preferred network setup to minimize page-in latency to host memory?
[11:05] Samira Khan: Keep the host memory local to the GPU instance and use high-bandwidth NVMe for spill. Avoid network-attached host storage for hot page-ins; it adds jitter.
[11:16] Jia Li: For compliance, can we disable host spill entirely so nothing goes to disk?
[11:20] Alex Perkins: Yes, you can set spill_to_disk=false and allow only host memory; if host memory is insufficient, generator will fall back to recompute path which may increase latency. We'll document tradeoffs.
[11:33] Marcos Rivera: Recompute path — meaning we recompute KV on the fly? That sounds expensive.
[11:36] Samira Khan: It's recompute for very old prefixes we chose not to spill. It increases CPU/GPU load but avoids persisting sensitive context. Often used by customers with strict data residency.
[11:46] Alex Perkins: Quick demo segue — Samira will show a snippet of telemetry and a simulated run with our bench tool.
[11:51] Samira Khan: (screen share) here's our bench: we replayed a 1h trace and instrumented cache_hit, eviction, page-in heatmap. You can see two large troughs at 02:15 and 03:40 that correspond to ingestion jobs. When we raised hot_pool_size by 30% the p95 dropped from 420ms to 310ms but cost (GPU mem allocation) rose ~18%.
[12:24] Marcos Rivera: That's useful. Can you share the exact config you used?
[12:27] Samira Khan: Yep — hot_pool_size, ttl_window=7200s, pin_list of top 5% accounts, batch_max=16, quant=8bit. We'll push the config and the raw bench CSV.
[12:40] Priya Desai: Anything else about prefix reuse patterns?
[12:43] Samira Khan: If prefix hashing is stable and TTL is long enough, reuse should be high. Also avoid regenerating session-ids each request — keep session affinity for the duration you expect reuse.
[12:54] Marcos Rivera: For long-term, what's the roadmap for more advanced eviction policies?
[12:58] Samira Khan: We're working on an adaptive hybrid policy that incorporates recency, frequency, and predictive weights from prefetch signals. ETA Q3 2026 for alpha.
[13:08] Ethan Cole: Great. Any quick wins to implement this week?
[13:11] Samira Khan: Quick wins: canonicalize prefixes, lengthen TTL, pin top-N accounts, and schedule ingestion off-peak or to a separate pool. We'll send a checklist.
[13:19] Alex Perkins: Let's do a recap and owners.
[13:22] Marcos Rivera: Recap from Helios side: we'll upload traces, try lengthening TTL in staging, and evaluate pre-warm.
[13:30] Alex Perkins: Redwood will share bench sheet, sample pre-warm scripts, and a recommended config. Samira will propose the pilot scope.
[13:36] Priya Desai: Security follow-up: Jia and Alex to sync on encryption of spilled KV and audit logging.
[13:42] Jia Li: Yes, will add questions to the security doc.
[13:45] Alex Perkins: Thanks everyone, we'll send notes and follow-up items.
[13:49] Marcos Rivera: Thanks all.

End of call.
notes: References: /drive/kv-cache-benchmarks.xlsx, shared pre-warm script link, Redwood KV cache ops doc. Transcript contains typical ASR artifacts (tokenization, minor mis-hears).
